strengths: The paper makes a coherent and mathematically careful contribution: it reformulates Wahba's problem in complex projective space via SU(2)/stereographic projection, deriving linear constraints on quaternion parameters (Eqs. 20-38) with a full metric derivation and edge-case proofs in the supplementary material, which is a genuinely interesting theoretical perspective on a classical problem.

The minimal-case results are practically valuable: the noiseless two-point closed-form solution (Eqs. 41-42) with systematic kernel-row selection handles singular configurations more rigorously than prior simple estimators, and the weighted two-point solution (Eq. 43) uses unnormalized quaternion averaging to reduce operation counts (~1/3 the multiplications of QUEST/Fast-Quat in the unweighted case, Table 2).

Experiments are unusually thorough for this type of contribution: 1 million Monte Carlo trials per configuration against five classical solvers (Q-method, QUEST, ESOQ2, FLAE, OLAE), 24 learning configurations across losses, learning rates, dimensions, real/complex networks, plus a small vision task, with full results and timings in the supplement.

The proposed representations are compared fairly against strong recent baselines (Gram-Schmidt 6D, QCQP, SVD-based rotation regression), and the paper is honest about where its methods do not win (e.g., the noisy Möbiius approximation G_M in Table 1/5, mixed test results in Table 4, unclear relative strengths of QMAlg vs. QMSVD).

The 2-vec representation is a clean, well-motivated improvement over Gram-Schmidt: it replaces greedy orthogonalization with the optimal two-point Wahba solution, balances error across both predicted axes, and shows consistent empirical gains (Tables 3, 4, Figure 2) with notably fast inference.
weaknesses: The significance of the deep learning contribution is modest. The QuadMobius representations achieve accuracy essentially on par with existing QCQP and SVD methods (Tables 3 and 4), at higher computational cost (Table 7), and the general Möbiius approximation is actually less accurate on the underlying estimation problem (Table 1). The claimed benefit is a 'potentially more flexible' representation, which is speculative and not convincingly demonstrated.

The gains of the proposed representations over existing ones are small and sometimes inconsistent (e.g., 2-vec loses to QCQP/SVD on many trials in Table 6; test-set results in Table 4 'correlated weakly with validation results'), and the paper cannot clearly articulate when each representation would be preferred.

Evaluation on the learning side is limited to synthetic Wahba-style regression and one small NeRF camera-orientation task on a lightweight backbone; there is no evidence on established rotation-estimation benchmarks (e.g., point cloud registration, pose estimation datasets) that would establish broader impact for the proposed representations.

The core insight—that quaternion parameters act linearly under Möbius/SU(2) maps—is closely connected to well-known results (Bingham/QCQP-style methods in [8, 21], Olkin-type linear estimators such as OLAE [19]), and the optimal solvers necessarily recover the same solution as Davenport's Q-method, so the algorithmic novelty for the general n-point case is mainly a different derivation rather than a new solution.

The paper mixes two contributions (classical Wahba solvers and neural rotation representations) without a unified application story; the classical solvers are not used in the neural pipeline in a way that demonstrates their practical synergy, and portions of the material (one-point case, degenerate-case details) feel like a technical report rather than a focused conference contribution.

strengths: Mathematically rigorous: the derivations connecting SU(2)/stereographic projection to Wahba's problem are careful, and the supplementary material contains complete proofs (metric in complex projective space, nearest special unitary matrix, two-point optimality), which is a point in the paper's favor.

The two-point solvers are practically relevant: Table 2/5 show the proposed methods match optimal existing solvers while requiring roughly one-third of the multiplications in the unweighted case, with a systematic singularity-avoidance scheme (Sec. 3.2) that is a genuine engineering contribution.

The 2-vec representation is a simple, sensible improvement over Gram-Schmidt (symmetric rather than greedy axis prioritization), and the learning experiments (Tab. 3, 6, 7) show it is competitive with much heavier eigendecomposition-based representations at a fraction of the cost.
Evaluation of the Wahba solvers is statistically solid (1M trials, medians, comparisons against Q-method, QUEST, ESOQ2, FLAE, OLAE, and closed-form two-point estimators).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the central observation that quaternion parameters act linearly in complex projective space largely re-derives existing linear/quaternionic Wahba formulations (FLAE, OLAE, and Davenport's Q-method). Since SU(2) is isomorphic to unit quaternions, much of the paper reads as a change of notation over known results; the paper does not convincingly articulate what the SU(2) view enables that quaternion-based formulations already do not.

The headline general solver (G_P / G_S) matches prior work exactly in accuracy and is slower in wall-clock time (Tab. 5) than QUEST/FLAE/OLAE, so the claimed practical gain rests on a narrow case (n=2).

The Möbius approximation is strictly worse in accuracy (roughly 3x error across noise levels) and the slowest of the proposed solvers; its main justification is a vague claim that noise sensitivity 'could be a benefit' in learning, which is not substantiated.

The learning evaluation is confined to synthetic Wahba's problem and a very small vision experiment (one NeRF 'lego' scene, ~100 images, small backbone) with mixed and weakly correlated test results (Tab. 4), acknowledging overfitting. No standard rotation-regression benchmarks (e.g., point-cloud or pose datasets) are used, so the significance of the new representations beyond this narrow setup is unclear.

The QuadMobius 16D representation is presented as more flexible, but it trains/infers the slowest (Tab. 7), behaves inconsistently between algebraic and SVD variants ('unclear in which cases each might excel'), and the paper offers no analysis or guidance on when it is preferable to QCQP/SVD — the differences reported are within noise of trial-to-trial variance.

Positioning is somewhat overstated: claims of 'new representations' and 'several new formulas' amount to incremental variants of known constructions (Bingham/QCQP-style eigendecomposition maps, quaternion averaging from Markley et al.), and related linear estimation literature (e.g., OLAE) is cited but not differentiated in depth.

Overall scope/significance: the contributions are scattered across a classic estimation problem, marginal closed-form cases, and neural parameterizations, without a unified payoff; impact on any sub-area appears modest.

strengths: Technically solid and self-contained development: the paper carefully derives the chordal metric in complex projective space, shows that quaternion/SU(2) parameters act linearly on stereographic coordinates, and reduces Wahba's problem to an eigenvector problem (Eqs. 28, 38) with proofs provided in the supplementary material.

Practical closed-form contributions: the two-point solvers (Eqs. 41-44) are verified to match optimal results of QUEST/Fast Quat while requiring roughly a third of the multiplications in the unweighted case, a concrete and validated efficiency gain (Table 2, Table 5).
The kernel-based selection strategy for handling singular regions of two-point estimators (Sec. 3.2) is a clean and systematic improvement over existing ad-hoc condition checks.

Two new learning representations (2-vec and QuadMobius) are well motivated, come with differentiable backward formulations (Supp. Sec. B), and are evaluated against strong baselines (Gram-Schmidt, QCQP, SVD) across a large grid of 24 training configurations plus a vision task.

Experiments are extensive: 1 million trials per configuration for solver validation, full results, and timing comparisons in the supplementary; 2-vec shows consistently better results than Gram-Schmidt at equal dimensionality.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough, including proofs of the metric at the point at infinity, nearest-special-unitary projection, two-point optimality, degenerate cases, and backpropagation derivations.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the equivalence between quaternion/eigenvector-based solutions and the proposed SU(2) formulations is acknowledged by the authors themselves (the solvers provably recover Davenport's Q-method output). The core insight - that rotation parameters act linearly via Möbius/stereographic maps - is closely related to well-established connections between Möbius transformations, complex Bingham distributions, and attitude determination, so the general-case solver contributions amount largely to re-derivations from a new viewpoint.

The 2-vec representation is an incremental modification of the widely known 6D Gram-Schmidt representation [26]; the improvement is a Wahba-optimal balancing of the two axis predictions. While the empirical gains over Gram-Schmidt are consistent, the methodological delta is small.

The QuadMobius representations are computationally slower than QCQP/SVD (Table 7) and their accuracy advantage over the top baselines is marginal and not statistically characterized (single 'lowest error trial' highlighted in Table 3; mixed and weakly correlated validation/test results in Table 4 attributed to overfitting). The practical benefit over existing representations is not convincingly established.

Evaluation of the learning representations is confined to synthetic Wahba's problem and one small-scale camera orientation task on the NeRF 'lego' dataset with a lightweight backbone; no standard rotation estimation benchmarks (e.g., point cloud registration, relative pose on real data) are included, limiting evidence of broader significance.

The Möbius approximation (Sec. 2.3) is notably less accurate (roughly 3x error) and its main selling point - noise sensitivity as a learning inductive bias - is asserted rather than demonstrated, since no analysis or ablation links the approximation error to learning behavior.

Significance for the broader AI community is unclear: the paper sits at the intersection of classical aerospace attitude estimation and deep rotation learning, but the deepest contributions (two-point solvers, one-point kernel constructions) primarily target the former, while the learning portion offers only modest gains over mature baselines.

Several design choices are left as empirical observations rather than analyzed (e.g., 'it is unclear in which cases each [QuadMobius variant] might excel'), leaving a gap between the claimed flexibility of the complex representation and demonstrated understanding of when it helps.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent theory-to-application arc: elegant reformulation of Wahba's problem via SU(2)/complex projective space yields linear constraints on quaternion parameters, from which multiple concrete algorithms are derived.

The theoretical development is thorough and largely self-contained, with extensive appendix material including full proofs (metric in CP1, nearest-special-unitary projection, weighted/unweighted two-point optimality, degenerate cases, backpropagation derivatives).

The proposed Wahba solvers are validated against established quaternion solvers (QUEST, ESOQ2, FLAE, OLAE, Q-method) over one million trials and match optimal accuracy, and the two-point closed-form solutions are claimed and shown to be optimal with a meaningful efficiency gain (~1/3 the multiplications of prior methods).

The learning experiments are broad and use appropriate, strong baselines (Gram-Schmidt, QCQP, SVD, Euler, quaternion) across three public benchmarks (ModelNet10-SO3, inverse kinematics, Cambridge Landmarks), plus a large grid of synthetic learning trials, timing comparisons, and ablations (dropout resilience, gradient-magnitude analysis).

The paper goes beyond empirical gains to explain why the representations work: gradient ratio analysis for 2-vec vs. Gram-Schmidt and gradient distribution/ablation analysis for QuadMobius provide mechanistic support for the design choices.
2-vec is a practically attractive contribution: same dimensionality and cost as Gram-Schmidt but optimal in the Wahba sense, consistently outperforming it across tasks.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental in places. The SU(2)-quaternion connection is classical, and the derived linear quaternion constraints closely parallel existing work (e.g., FLAE/OLAE-style linear estimators); 2-vec is a direct modification of Zhou et al. (2019)'s Gram-Schmidt map, and QuadMobius is explicitly inspired by Levinson et al. (2020) and Peretroukhin et al. (2020).

The Möbius-approximation solver underlying QuadMobius is not optimal (Table 4 shows notably worse accuracy and much slower runtime for n=100 than QUEST/FLAE), which weakens the claim that this path is preferable for exact estimation; its value is only as a learning representation.

Empirical gains of the new representations over strong baselines are modest and sometimes within run-to-run noise; no statistical significance testing or multiple-seed variance reporting is provided for the benchmark experiments (ModelNet10 limited to three categories, Cambridge Landmarks limited to three scenes).
The paper does not clearly state code release, which limits reproducibility given the large number of bespoke derivations and C++ reimplementations.

The connection between the theoretical results and the learning representations is somewhat loose for QuadMobius, since the final map is an approximate projection rather than an optimal solver; the benefit of the SU(2) framing over simply treating the 16D output as a Hermitian matrix (which is essentially QCQP-style) could be articulated more sharply.
Some positioning gaps: comparisons to more recent rotation-regression methods (e.g., projective manifold gradient layer of Chen et al., 2022) are cited but not empirically compared.

strengths: Comprehensive and careful theoretical development: the derivation of linear quaternion constraints via SU(2) (Eqs. 11, 18) is technically sound and well-documented, with extensive proofs and derivations in the appendix.
The two-point closed-form solutions (Eqs. 20-22) are shown to be optimal in the Wahba's problem sense and simpler/faster than existing solvers (Table 5), with thoughtful handling of degenerate cases.
The 2-vec representation offers a principled, balanced alternative to Gram-Schmidt at essentially identical computational cost, with supporting gradient-balance analysis (Fig. 3).

Evaluation spans three standard benchmarks (ModelNet10-SO3, inverse kinematics, Cambridge Landmarks) plus synthetic Wahba's problem trials with many seeds/configurations, and includes timing comparisons.
QuadMobius probes (dropout resilience, gradient distributions, ablation in Table 3) show an honest attempt to understand why the representation works rather than only reporting wins.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central framing: the SU(2)-quaternion isomorphism and its relationship to SO(3) are classical, and the proposed optimal solvers (Eqs. 12, 19) are shown in Table 4 to be numerically equivalent to Davenport's Q-method while being slower than QUEST/FLAE/OLAE. The 'SU(2) lens' thus repackages known results without producing a better or faster general solver.

Empirical gains in the learning experiments are modest and inconsistent. In Tables 1 and 2, 2-vec frequently loses to baselines (e.g., GS/QCQP on Sofa) and QuadMobius variants only marginally beat QCQP/SVD, often within what appears to be run-to-run noise; no statistical significance testing or multiple-run variance is reported.

QuadMobius adds substantial cost (Table 7: ~2.5-4x inference time vs. QCQP/SVD) for small accuracy improvements, weakening the practical case; the justification that training-time differences are 'negligible' is unconvincing given the overhead.

The Möbius approximation (Section 2.2) is not optimal and its noise sensitivity (Table 4) is acknowledged but left unresolved; its adoption in QuadMobius is justified mainly empirically rather than theoretically.
No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned despite heavy reimplementation of baselines.

The paper reads as a collection of loosely connected results (Wahba solvers, two-point cases, axis priors, two learning representations), diluting focus; the strongest individual contribution (unweighted two-point formula) may be better suited to a specialized estimation/robotics venue, and significance for a broad AI audience is limited.

strengths: The paper develops a coherent and non-trivial theoretical framework: reformulating Wahba's problem in complex projective space via SU(2) yields linear constraints on quaternion parameters (Eqs. 11, 18), which is an elegant and practically useful construction.

The applications are genuinely valuable: closed-form residual formulations for IRLS/L1-type losses, constrained optimization with axis priors, and simplified two-point solutions (Eqs. 21-22) that appear optimal and cheaper than prior closed-form methods (Table 5), including a well-handled degenerate-case analysis.

Extensive and broad empirical evaluation: one million synthetic trials of Wahba solvers against QUEST/ESOQ2/FLAE/OLAE, three distinct learning benchmarks (ModelNet10-SO3, inverse kinematics, Cambridge Landmarks pose regression), plus synthetic learning experiments over 24 configurations with convergence/leader-count analysis.

The proposed representations (2-vec and QuadMobius) are competitive with or better than strong baselines (Gram-Schmidt, QCQP, SVD) across benchmarks, and the paper includes ablations (dropout resilience, gradient magnitude distributions, Table 3) that probe *why* QuadMobius works, not just that it does.

Careful supporting material: derivations of metrics, backpropagation formulas for the eigenvector and polar-decomposition steps (Section E), nearest-unitary-matrix proofs, and compute timings — the work is unusually thorough for the topic.
The writing is generally clear, and the connection between Wahba's-problem solvers and rotation representations for learning (Levinson et al. 2020; Peretroukhin et al. 2020) is well motivated.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the central idea — interpreting network outputs as matrices that map to rotations via Wahba's-problem solvers — is already established by Levinson et al. (2020) and Peretroukhin et al. (2020), and the paper acknowledges QuadMobius is 'motivated by ideas from' them. The genuinely new parts (linear quaternion constraints from SU(2), the Möbius relaxation) are technically interesting but incremental relative to this prior art, and linear quaternion estimators have close precedent in OLAE/FLAE.

Empirical gains are modest and inconsistently supported: in Table 1 and Table 2, the best method varies per dataset/metric with no error bars, repeated runs, or significance testing; differences of e.g. 13.68 vs 13.92 mean error, or QMAlg vs GS on Old Hospital (4.426 vs 4.295), are within plausible run-to-run variance. 2-vec actually underperforms GS in several settings (Sofa Acc5: 0.364 vs 0.441).

The Möbius-based solution (Section 2.2) is an approximation that is measurably suboptimal (Table 4: ~order-of-magnitude worse error at low noise and much slower at n=100), which weakens the claim of a principled SU(2) solution path, though the authors candidly note this.

The significance for a general AI audience is debatable: much of the paper (two-point closed forms, edge-case handling, operation counts) is squarely attitude-determination engineering, and the learning contribution rests on three smallish benchmarks; impact on the broader field is likely niche (rotation learning sub-area).

QuadMobius is substantially slower at inference (Table 7: ~2x QCQP, ~10x quaternion) and the higher-dimensional 16D map raises the question of whether gains come from added capacity rather than the representation itself; the paper does not fully disentangle this (e.g., a 16D real-valued control of equal dimensionality is not tested).
No mention of code release; given the many formulas and implementation choices (branching, degenerate-case handling, complex differentiation conventions), reproducibility is a concern.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'this map is motivated by ideas from ... offering a potentially more flexible learning representation' — 'potentially' is appropriate, but the abstract/conclusion state effectiveness more confidently than the mixed tables justify.
